analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from using AI and personal data to charge individual customers personalized prices or set individual workers' pay.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in three House committees since its July 2025 introduction, with no action, no hearing scheduled in the record, and no Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for companies to use automated systems fed by personal or "surveillance" data — things like location, behavior, genetics, or purchased data profiles — to set a custom price for an individual customer or to determine what an individual worker is paid. Companies could still offer real cost-based differences, disclosed uniform discounts to groups like seniors or teachers, and pay systems based only on local cost of living. It would be enforced by the FTC and, for wages, the EEOC, and it would let consumers and workers sue for at least $3,000 per violation, with arbitration bans and class-action waivers unenforceable for these claims. State laws giving stronger protections would be preserved, and collective bargaining over pay algorithms would remain intact.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers. Shoppers would stop paying prices tuned to what a company knows about them personally, and workers would be shielded from pay-setting software that prices individual labor down using personal data. People could sue violators for at least $3,000 per violation and cannot be forced into arbitration for these claims.

how_it_helps.text: Bans companies from using automated systems to set an individualized price for a specific person or group based on surveillance data — information gathered or bought about their traits, behavior, genetics, or biometrics — with narrow exceptions for cost-based differences and publicly disclosed uniform discounts.

Bans employers from using automated systems that consider personal or surveillance data to set or inform a worker's pay, scheduling, or task assignments, allowing only location-based cost-of-living data.
Requires companies to publish, before using these systems, how the data is used, and gives consumers and workers a process to correct or challenge inaccurate data about themselves.

Lets injured consumers and workers sue for at least $3,000 per violation (tripled for willful violations), with attorney's fees, and bars companies from forcing these disputes into pre-dispute arbitration or waiving class actions.
Enforced by the FTC, the EEOC, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits, and preserves stronger state laws and collective bargaining agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that use AI-driven, data-based individualized pricing and pay — large retailers, e-commerce platforms, and gig and HR software firms — would face a federal ban on those practices, FTC and EEOC enforcement, state attorney general suits, and lawsuits from consumers and workers with minimum damages per violation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retailers, platforms, and employers using pricing/pay algorithms

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches nearly any use of personal or acquired data in pricing or pay, not just clearly invasive practices, so it could restrict pricing tools that benefit consumers, such as legitimate personalized discounts, and create compliance uncertainty for businesses of all sizes.

The private right of action with $3,000-per-violation minimum damages and mandatory attorney's fees, plus the invalidation of pre-dispute arbitration, could generate a wave of litigation that some businesses would contest as burdensome and that courts would have to sort out.

Employers must publish procedures and give 180 days' notice before using automated systems to inform wages, which imposes administrative costs, though the bill expressly allows pay based only on local cost of living and preserves collective bargaining.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection upside is real: individually tailored prices based on personal data can quietly charge people more based on what companies know about them, and algorithmic pay tools have been credibly criticized for suppressing wages. The main costs fall on businesses, which would face compliance duties (publishing procedures, giving advance notice before using pay algorithms) and new litigation exposure under a $3,000-per-violation private right of action with fee-shifting — a structure that some firms argue invites abusive suits. Defining "surveillance data" broadly enough to cover any acquired information also raises questions about how companies can price or pay at all while staying compliant, which could make the rules harder to follow than intended. On balance, the bill's burden falls on firms, and its protections run to consumers and workers; the enforcement design is aggressive and could have benefited from narrower scoping.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees in July 2025, and nothing has happened to it since — no markup, no vote, nothing in the record.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 23, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Education and Workforce Committees.
No further action appears in the record since the referrals: no committee markup, no hearing, and no floor vote are listed.
All 41 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, the bill has no path forward in this Congress as it stands.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, companies that use personal data and AI to set individualized prices and wages are better off: the bill is stalled in committee and nothing restricts those practices yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms using personalized pricing and pay algorithms

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban surveillance-based price setting and wage setting.

for.name: Rep. Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Joined Casar as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none are Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill has gotten no movement in any of its three committees.

industries.note: The bill bans using purchased or acquired surveillance data for individualized pricing or pay, cutting off a market for selling personal data into pricing decisions. Ordinary consumers keep more of their wallet and privacy.

industries.industry: Large retailers, e-commerce platforms, and consumer brands
industries.note: Retailers and platforms that use AI to tune prices to individual shoppers would have to abandon that practice or restrict it to disclosed, uniform discounts. Consumers avoid being charged more based on their data profile.

industries.industry: Payroll, HR software, and gig-economy algorithmic pay firms
industries.note: Software that computes individual pay from worker data would be barred, though simple cost-of-living-based tools remain allowed. Workers gain protection from data-driven pay suppression.

industries.industry: AI software developers selling pricing and pay tools
industries.note: Vendors of algorithmic pricing and compensation systems face a restricted or eliminated market for surveillance-based products, while demand shifts toward compliant, location-only pay tools.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no recorded committee action, and no hearings in the record, the likely path is that the bill stays in its three committees and dies at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, as most bills referred to multiple committees do.
